chapter: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
title: Why the mambo overtook Afro-Cuban jazz
summary: Machito says mambo spread because American dance teachers made a dance for it, and anything danceable beat music to listen to.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Okay, all right, so there's no rhythms that you can say that "Asia Minor" and the rest of them were Afro-Cuban jazz, then. Tell me the truth, which was more exciting, the mambo or the Afro-Cuban jazz things?
Why did the mambo then catch on and eventually topped Afro-Cuban jazz in popularity?

Because the American teachers or dance teachers, they learned or they create a dance for Americans to the mambo and the people --- any music that you could dance with is more popular than the one that you had to listen to. In those days, the big band era, yeah, it was fading, but still in the mind of the people to dance the fox-trot, with Benny Goodman, Tommy Dorsey, you name it, all those big bands that it was so beautiful, so pleasant to dance.
Listen, the greatest thing in the world is to have a lady in your arms and could listen to "I Got You Under my Skin" or "Stairway To the Stars"; it's so romantic, so beautiful and that contact dance was so inspiring that anything that you could dance with was popular in those days. Tango, even Conga.
